subject: physics

sections.title: Introduction to Electric Charge and Electric Field
learning_objectives: Define electric charge, and describe how the two types of charge interact.

sections.title: Static Electricity and Charge: Conservation of Charge
learning_objectives: Define electric charge, and describe how the two types of charge interact.
Describe three common situations that generate static electricity.
State the law of conservation of charge.

sections.title: Conductors and Insulators
learning_objectives: Define conductor and insulator, explain the difference, and give examples of each.
Describe three methods for charging an object.
Explain what happens to an electric force as you move farther from the source.
Define polarization.

sections.title: Coulomb’s Law
learning_objectives: State Coulomb’s law in terms of how the electrostatic force changes with the distance between two objects.
Calculate the electrostatic force between two charged point forces, such as electrons or protons.

sections.title: Electric Field: Concept of a Field Revisited
learning_objectives: Describe a force field and calculate the strength of an electric field due to a point charge.
Calculate the force exerted on a test charge by an electric field.

sections.title: Electric Field Lines: Multiple Charges
learning_objectives: Calculate the total force (magnitude and direction) exerted on a test charge from more than one charge
Describe an electric field diagram of a positive point charge; of a negative point charge with twice the magnitude of positive charge
Draw the electric field lines between two points of the same charge; between two points of opposite charge.

sections.title: Electric Forces in Biology
learning_objectives: Describe how a water molecule is polar.
Explain electrostatic screening by a water molecule within a living cell.

sections.title: Conductors and Electric Fields in Static Equilibrium
learning_objectives: List the three properties of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
Explain the effect of an electric field on free charges in a conductor.
Explain why no electric field may exist inside a conductor.
Describe the electric field surrounding Earth.
Explain what happens to an electric field applied to an irregular conductor.
Describe how a lightning rod works.
Explain how a metal car may protect passengers inside from the dangerous electric fields caused by a downed line touching the car.

sections.title: Applications of Electrostatics
learning_objectives: Name several real-world applications of the study of electrostatics.

sections.title: Introduction to Electric Potential and Electric Energy
learning_objectives: Define electric potential and electric potential energy.

sections.title: Electric Potential Energy: Potential Difference
learning_objectives: Define electric potential and electric potential energy.
Describe the relationship between potential difference and electrical potential energy.
Explain electron volt and its usage in submicroscopic process.
Determine electric potential energy given potential difference and amount of charge.

sections.title: Electric Potential in a Uniform Electric Field
learning_objectives: Describe the relationship between voltage and electric field.
Derive an expression for the electric potential and electric field.
Calculate electric field strength given distance and voltage.

sections.title: Electrical Potential Due to a Point Charge
learning_objectives: Explain point charges and express the equation for electric potential of a point charge.
Distinguish between electric potential and electric field.
Determine the electric potential of a point charge given charge and distance.

sections.title: Equipotential Lines

Describe the action of grounding an electrical appliance.
Compare electric field and equipotential lines.

sections.title: Capacitors and Dielectrics

Identify series and parallel parts in the combination of connection of capacitors.
Calculate the effective capacitance in series and parallel given individual capacitances.

sections.title: Energy Stored in Capacitors
learning_objectives: List some uses of capacitors.
Express in equation form the energy stored in a capacitor.
Explain the function of a defibrillator.

misconception.text: Rubbing an isolated body leaves it with a net charge.

correction.text: Charge is conserved. Rubbing moves charge from one part of the body to another, so the total charge of an isolated body stays zero even though its parts are now charged.

signal.text: Our own question asks what the total charge of an isolated body is.

misconception.text: The electrostatic force between two charges is inversely proportional to the distance between them.

correction.text: It is inversely proportional to the square of the distance, so doubling the separation makes the force a quarter as large.

signal.text: Our own question offers the inverse-distance law as an option.

misconception.text: Potential difference between two points is the force on a unit charge placed between them.

correction.text: That is the electric field. The potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between the two points.

signal.text: Our own question offers the field definition as an option.

misconception.text: The potential of a point charge falls with the square of the distance, like the field.

correction.text: The potential falls as $1/r$. It is the electric field that falls as $1/r^2$, because the field is the gradient of the potential.

signal.text: Our own question offers the square law as an option.

stem.text: The total charge of an isolated body is

options.text: equal to the number of electrons it has lost

explanation.text: Charge is conserved. An isolated body that becomes charged has simply moved some charge from one part of itself to another, so the total stays zero.

stem.text: A metal rod and a rubber rod are both rubbed with silk. The metal

options.text: becomes positively charged and the rubber negatively charged
becomes negatively charged and the rubber positively charged

explanation.text: Rubbing transfers electrons. The metal loses electrons and becomes positive; the rubber gains them and becomes negative.

stem.text: The electrostatic force between two charges is

options.text: independent of the distance between them
inversely proportional to the square of the distance

explanation.text: Coulomb's law gives $F = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$, so the force falls off with the square of the separation.

stem.text: The potential difference between two points is

options.text: the force per unit charge between them
the work done per unit charge in moving a charge between them
the energy of a charge at the first point

explanation.text: Potential difference is the work done per unit charge in moving a test charge between the two points.

stem.text: In a uniform electric field, the potential difference between two points a distance $d$ apart along the field is

explanation.text: The work done per unit charge over a distance $d$ along the field is $Ed$.

stem.text: The potential at a distance $r$ from a point charge $q$ is proportional to

explanation.text: The potential falls as $V = kq/r$, so it is inversely proportional to the distance. The field, by contrast, falls as $1/r^2$.
